content: 1. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for infants exposed to HIV starting at 4 to 6 weeks of age. This prophylaxis should continue until HIV infection is definitively ruled out using an age-appropriate HIV test after breastfeeding has completely ceased. This recommendation is strong, although the evidence supporting it is of very low certainty. 2. Routine co-trimoxazole prophylaxis should be provided to all individuals living with HIV who have active tuberculosis (TB) disease, regardless of their CD4 cell count. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-certainty evidence. 3. People living with HIV should be systematically screened for TB disease at every visit to a healthcare facility. This is a strong recommendation, but the evidence supporting it is of very low certainty. 4. For adults and adolescents living with HIV, systematic TB screening should use the WHO-recommended four-symptom screen. Individuals reporting any of the following symptoms—current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats—should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 5. For children under 10 years of age living with HIV, TB screening should include symptoms such as current cough, fever, poor weight gain, or close contact with someone with TB disease. This is a strong recommendation, but the evidence for test accuracy is of low certainty. 6. Among adults and adolescents living with HIV, C-reactive protein (CRP) testing with a cutoff of >5 mg/L may be used to screen for TB disease. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence for test accuracy. 7. Chest X-rays may be used to screen for TB disease in adults and adolescents living with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for test accuracy. 8. For individuals aged 15 years and older in populations where TB screening is recommended, computer-aided detection software may be used to interpret digital chest X-rays instead of human readers. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 9. Molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests may be used to screen for TB disease in adults and adolescents living with HIV. This is a conditional recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence for test accuracy. 10. The WHO recommends antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all individuals with HIV and drug-resistant TB who require second-line anti-TB drugs. ART should be initiated as early as possible, ideally within the first eight weeks of starting anti-TB treatment. This is a strong recommendation, but the evidence is of very low certainty. 11. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB should receive TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care. This includes those on ART, pregnant women, and individuals previously treated for TB, regardless of the degree of immunosuppression or availability of latent TB infection testing. This is a strong recommendation supported by high-certainty evidence. 12. Infants under 12 months of age living with HIV who are in contact with someone with TB and are unlikely to have active TB based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines should receive TB preventive treatment. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 13. Children aged 12 months or older living with HIV who are unlikely to have active TB based on clinical evaluation or national guidelines should be offered TB preventive treatment as part of comprehensive HIV care, especially in settings with high TB transmission. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 14. All children living with HIV who have successfully completed treatment for TB disease may be offered TB preventive treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 15. Adults and adolescents living with HIV should be screened for TB using a clinical algorithm. Those without symptoms such as current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats are unlikely to have active TB and should be offered preventive treatment, regardless of their ART status. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 16. Adults and adolescents living with HIV who report any of the symptoms of current cough, fever, weight loss, or night sweats during TB screening should be evaluated for TB and other diseases. If active TB is excluded, they should be offered preventive treatment. This is a strong recommendation with moderate-certainty evidence. 17. Chest radiography may be offered to individuals living with HIV who are receiving ART and TB preventive treatment, provided there are no abnormal radiographic findings. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 18. Infants and children living with HIV who exhibit poor weight gain, fever, current cough, or a history of contact with someone with TB should be evaluated for TB and other diseases causing these symptoms. If active TB is excluded, they should be offered TB preventive treatment regardless of age. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 19. The absence of TB symptoms and normal chest radiographic findings may be used to rule out active TB disease in HIV-negative household contacts aged 5 years or older and other at-risk groups before initiating TB preventive treatment. This is a conditional recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 20. Testing for latent TB infection can be performed using either a tuberculin skin test or an interferon-gamma release assay. This is a strong recommendation with very low-certainty evidence. 21. Recommended treatment options for latent TB infection include six or nine months of daily isoniazid, a three-month regimen of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid, or a three-month regimen of daily isoniazid plus rifampicin. This is a strong recommendation with moderateto high-certainty evidence. 22. Alternative regimens for latent TB infection include a one-month regimen of daily rifapentine plus isoniazid or four months of daily rifampicin alone. These are conditional recommendations with lowto moderate-certainty evidence. 23. In settings with high TB transmission, adults and adolescents living with HIV who have a positive or unknown latent TB infection test and are unlikely to have active TB disease should receive at least 36 months of daily isoniazid preventive therapy. This should be provided regardless of ART status, degree of immunosuppression, history of previous TB treatment, or pregnancy. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 24. In settings with an HBsAg seroprevalence of ≥2% or ≥5% in the general population, all adults and adolescents should have routine access to HBsAg serological testing with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. This is a conditional recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 25. Pregnant women in settings with an HBsAg seroprevalence of ≥2% or ≥5% should be routinely offered HBsAg serological testing during antenatal care, with linkage to prevention, care, and treatment services. This is a strong recommendation with low-certainty evidence. 26. All infants should receive their first dose of the HBV vaccine as soon as possible after birth, preferably within 24 hours.
